passages.context: Latham's reconstruction of what the apostles saw, read on printed page 34 rendered from the hashed facsimile. Registered as the origin of the modern collapsed-cloths reading; on the following page Latham writes that he has nearly repeated Mr Beard's view.
passages.notes: Latham's footnote on this page notes the Revised Version's linen cloths against the older linen clothes. The reconstruction is Latham's inference; the Gospel text says none of it, and consuming publications must not report it as description.

passages.context: Latham on the participle at John 20:7, read on printed page 43 rendered from the hashed facsimile. Registered because a proponent of the arrangement argument here states against interest that the Greek does not mean folded.
passages.notes: The printing sets the participle entetyligmenon in Greek type in parenthesis after rolled up; it is omitted from this transcription, which carries no Greek. Latham's footnotes on the same page give the Greek of John 20:6 and 20:7 and the remark that the word apart is emphasised. Two pages later, at printed page 45, Latham writes that the Greek word used about the napkin does not imply a folding up for neatness' sake.

work.author: Henry Latham
work.description: Latham's 1901 study of the resurrection narratives, whose second and third chapters propose that the burial cloths in the empty tomb were found collapsed where the body had lain, with the head-cloth retaining the annular form given it by the head. Latham credits the central idea to a pamphlet by the Rev. Arthur Beard of St John's College, Cambridge, which has not been located. The proposal is the ancestor of most later English writing on the disposition of the cloths. A locus is the chapter.
work.title: The Risen Master: A Sequel to Pastor Pastorum
